sources.news_title: How the Increase in Traffic Accidents Is Linked to the Release of New Music Albums
sources.text:
ΗΠΑ: Πώς συνδέεται η αύξηση των τροχαίων δυστυχημάτων με την κυκλοφορία νέων μουσικών άλμπουμ
Στην εποχή της ψηφιακής υπερσύνδεσης, η αλληλεπίδρασή μας με την τεχνολογία έχει εισχωρήσει ακόμη και στις πιο καθημερινές μας συνήθειες, όπως η οδήγηση. Ενώ οι κίνδυνοι από τη συνομιλία ή τη σύνταξη γραπτών μηνυμάτων εν ώρα οδήγησης είναι ευρέως γνωστοί, μια νέα, απρόσμενη απειλή έρχεται στο φως...
- «Αυτό είναι πρωτοφανές»: Γιατί οι πρόσφατες αποκαλύψεις του Πενταγώνου για τα UFO είναι τόσο σημαντικές
- Συνελήφθησαν τρεις γυναίκες που έκλεβαν ρούχα από εμπορικά καταστήματα στο κέντρο της Αθήνας
- Ο πρόεδρος γερμανικής start-up που προμηθεύει με drones την Ουκρανία, κρύβεται επειδή φοβάται την Ρωσία
- Τα ΗΑΕ κατηγορούν το Ιράν ότι εκτόξευσε δύο πυραύλους εναντίον τους – Έστειλαν τους πολίτες στα καταφύγια
Η εικόνα είναι οικεία σε όλους μας: ένα ηλιόλουστο απόγευμα, ένας ανοιχτός δρόμος, τα χέρια στο τιμόνι και το ολοκαίνουργιο τραγούδι του αγαπημένου μας καλλιτέχνη να παίζει στο ηχοσύστημα του αυτοκινήτου μέσω του κινητού μας τηλεφώνου.
Για τους περισσότερους οδηγούς, η αναπαραγωγή μουσικής στο αυτοκίνητο θεωρείται μια αθώα, σχεδόν αυτόματη συνήθεια. Ωστόσο, μια επιστημονική μελέτη από ερευνητές της Ιατρικής Σχολής του Χάρβαρντ (Harvard Medical School) αποκαλύπτει μια σκοτεινή και απρόσμενη πραγματικότητα: τις ημέρες που κυκλοφορούν τα πιο δημοφιλή μουσικά άλμπουμ, τα τροχαία δυστυχήματα σημειώνουν κατακόρυφη αύξηση.
Πρόσφατη επιστημονική μελέτη αποκαλύπτει μια εντυπωσιακή και ανησυχητική συσχέτιση: τις ημέρες που κυκλοφορούν τα πιο δημοφιλή μουσικά άλμπουμ, τα θανατηφόρα τροχαία σημειώνουν κατακόρυφη αύξηση
Η έρευνα, η οποία ανέλυσε εκατοντάδες χιλιάδες συμβάντα στις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες, συνδέει την έξαρση της χρήσης των smartphones για online μουσική με τη διάσπαση της προσοχής των οδηγών, αναδεικνύοντας μια σύγχρονη απειλή για την οδική ασφάλεια.
Τα αριθμητικά δεδομένα της έρευνας
Για να κατανοήσουν τη σχέση μεταξύ της ψηφιακής ψυχαγωγίας και των κινδύνων στον δρόμο, οι ερευνητές εξέτασαν συνολικά 233.809 θανατηφόρα τροχαία δυστυχήματα που καταγράφηκαν στο επίσημο αμερικανικό μητρώο FARS (Fatality Analysis Reporting System) από την 1η Ιανουαρίου 2017 έως τις 31 Δεκεμβρίου 2022.
Η μεθοδολογία της μελέτης βασίστηκε σε ένα «πρωτότυπο πείραμα». Οι επιστήμονες επέλεξαν τις ημέρες κυκλοφορίας των 10 πιο δημοφιλών άλμπουμ της εξαετίας -όπως για παράδειγμα νέες κυκλοφορίες με εκατομμύρια αναπαραγωγές από την πρώτη κιόλας ημέρα- και συνέκριναν τους θανάτους στους δρόμους με μια απόκλιση δέκα ημερών πριν και δέκα ημερών μετά από κάθε κυκλοφορία.
Τα ευρήματα ήταν αποκαλυπτικά :
- Έκρηξη στο streaming: Τις ημέρες κυκλοφορίας των μεγάλων άλμπουμ, ο όγκος αναπαραγωγής μουσικής στις πλατφόρμες (όπως το Spotify) αυξήθηκε κατά 43% (από 86,1 εκατομμύρια streams κατά μέσο όρο τις υπόλοιπες ημέρες, στα 123,3 εκατομμύρια).
- Άλμα στα θανατηφόρα τροχαία: Τις ίδιες ακριβώς ημέρες, ο αριθμός των θυμάτων από τροχαία αυξήθηκε από 120,9 σε 139,1 θανάτους ημερησίως.
- Η στατιστική επιβάρυνση: Αυτό μεταφράζεται σε μια σχετική αύξηση 15,1% στα θανατηφόρα δυστυχήματα. Συνολικά, υπολογίζεται ότι περίπου 182 επιπλέον άνθρωποι έχασαν τη ζωή τους στις ΗΠΑ.
Γιατί συμβαίνει αυτό; Ο μηχανισμός της διάσπασης
Ενώ η συνομιλία στο τηλέφωνο και τα γραπτά μηνύματα είναι ευρέως αναγνωρισμένες αιτίες ατυχημάτων, η διαχείριση της μουσικής θεωρείται λανθασμένα από τους οδηγούς ως μια δραστηριότητα χαμηλού κινδύνου. Ωστόσο, η χρήση του smartphone για την εύρεση, την επιλογή ή την αλλαγή τραγουδιών την ώρα της οδήγησης απαιτεί τριπλή ταυτόχρονη απόσπαση:
Οπτική: Ο οδηγός παίρνει τα μάτια του από τον δρόμο για να κοιτάξει την οθόνη του κινητού ή του ταμπλό.
Χειρωνακτική: Αφήνει το τιμόνι για να αγγίξει την οθόνη.
Γνωστική: Ο εγκέφαλος εστιάζει στην αναζήτηση του νέου άλμπουμ ή στη μουσική εμπειρία αντί για την οδήγηση.
Όπως σημειώνουν οι ερευνητές, η ταυτόχρονη διάθεση νέου ελκυστικού περιεχομένου δημιουργεί μια παρόρμηση στους χρήστες να αλληλεπιδράσουν αμέσως με την εφαρμογή, ακόμη κι αν βρίσκονται πίσω από το τιμόνι.
Ποιοι οδηγοί και ποιες συνθήκες κινδυνεύουν περισσότερο;
Η ενδελεχής ανάλυση των δεδομένων αποκάλυψε ότι η αύξηση των τροχαίων τις ημέρες των άλμπουμ δεν διανέμεται ομοιόμορφα, αλλά παρουσιάζει συγκεκριμένα χαρακτηριστικά:
Δημογραφικά χαρακτηριστικά
Νέοι οδηγοί: Η αύξηση των θανάτων ήταν σημαντικά μεγαλύτερη στις ηλικίες κάτω των 40 ετών. Αυτό εξηγείται από το γεγονός ότι οι νεότερες ηλικίες είναι οι κατεξοχήν χρήστες των υπηρεσιών streaming (πάνω από το 80% των ατόμων 12-34 ετών χρησιμοποιούν τέτοιες πλατφόρμες).
 Φύλο: Οι άνδρες οδηγοί σημείωσαν πολύ μεγαλύτερη αύξηση στα θανατηφόρα ατυχήματα σε σύγκριση με τις γυναίκες.
Συνθήκες οδήγησης και οχήματος
Μόνοι στο αυτοκίνητο: Τα δυστυχήματα αυξήθηκαν δραματικά σε οχήματα με έναν μόνο επιβαίνοντα. Όταν υπάρχει συνεπιβάτης, είναι πιθανό να αναλαμβάνει εκείνος τη διαχείριση της μουσικής ή να κρατά τον οδηγό σε εγρήγορση μέσω της κουβέντας. Ο μόνος οδηγός αναγκάζεται να κάνει τα πάντα μόνος του.
Καλός καιρός: Αντίθετα με αυτό που θα περίμενε κανείς, η έξαρση των θανατηφόρων σημειώθηκε τις ημέρες με αίθριο καιρό. Η εξήγηση των αναλυτών είναι πως όταν οι οδικές συνθήκες είναι ιδανικές, οι οδηγοί «χαλαρώνουν τη προσοχή τους» και θεωρούν ασφαλέστερο να ασχοληθούν με το κινητό τους.
Νηφάλιοι οδηγοί: Η αύξηση δεν οφειλόταν στο αλκοόλ, καθώς παρατηρήθηκε κυρίως σε οδηγούς που ήταν απόλυτα νηφάλιοι. Αυτό αποκλείει το σενάριο ότι οι θάνατοι αυξήθηκαν λόγω κατανάλωσης αλκοόλ.
Συστήματα infotainment: Τα νεότερα οχήματα εξοπλισμένα με ψηφιακές οθόνες ψυχαγωγίας (infotainment) παρουσίασαν επίσης υψηλότερα ποσοστά εμπλοκής. Παρότι οι οθόνες αυτές σχεδιάστηκαν για μεγαλύτερη ασφάλεια, τελικά μπορεί να μειώνουν το εμπόδιο για αλληλεπίδραση με τις εφαρμογές, προκαλώντας τελικά μεγαλύτερη απόσπαση.
Αποκλείοντας τις συμπτώσεις
Για να διασφαλίσουν ότι τα ευρήματά τους δεν ήταν απλές συμπτώσεις, οι ερευνητές διεξήγαγαν αυστηρούς ελέγχους:
Η «παγίδα» της Παρασκευής: Επειδή τα περισσότερα άλμπουμ κυκλοφορούν Παρασκευή (ημέρα που αυξάνεται γενικά η μετακίνηση), η μελέτη συνέκρινε τις Παρασκευές των άλμπουμ με τις προηγούμενες και επόμενες Παρασκευές. Η αύξηση παρέμεινε σταθερή και στατιστικά σημαντική.
Τυχαίες ημερομηνίες: Προσομοιώσεις με 1.000 τυχαίες ημερομηνίες έδειξαν ότι η πιθανότητα να οφείλεται αυτό το φαινόμενο στην τύχη είναι ελάχιστη (κάτω από 2%).
Έλεγχος εορτών: Εξετάστηκαν οι ίδιες ημερομηνίες σε άλλα έτη (χωρίς κυκλοφορία άλμπουμ) και δεν παρατηρήθηκε καμία αύξηση, αποκλείοντας το ενδεχόμενο να ευθύνεται κάποια εποχική ταξιδιωτική κίνηση.

sources.news_title: Taylor Swift, Drake And Bad Bunny Album Releases Linked To Rise In Fatal Car Crashes, According To Study
sources.text:
Major album releases on streaming services by artists like Taylor Swift, Drake, and Bad Bunny have been linked to a rise in fatal car crashes in the United States.
The study, published on Monday in the medical journal JAMA Network Open, examined the ten albums with the most first-day Spotify streams between 2017 and 2022, including Taylor Swift’s Midnights, Drake’s Certified Lover Boy, and Bad Bunny’s Un Verano Sin Ti. The study also included albums by Kendrick Lamar, Harry Styles, and Kanye West.
Although this data did not indicate whether listeners streamed the music in their car, the researchers found that the top 200 songs in the U.S. had streaming volumes 43% higher on the day of major album launches than on the days before the releases.
“What it establishes is that these days are genuinely different in terms of national engagement with music, which is the premise the whole study rests on,” said Patel.
The study examined a 10-day period before and after each album release. Using Spotify data, the researchers found that major album release days averaged 123.3 million streams, while days around the album’s release averaged 86.1 million. The researchers also examined drivers’ ages, alcohol use, the number of passengers in the vehicle, and the model year of the vehicles in fatal collisions.
On the days that the albums were released, around 15% more traffic fatalities occurred
According to the study, there were, on average, 121 fatal vehicle crashes on non-album release days, compared with 139 on album release days. Younger drivers also had fatal traffic accidents at a higher rate than senior drivers.
“What convinced me it was real was the pattern underneath it,” Patel told CNN. “The increase showed up mostly among drivers who were alone in the car, it was more pronounced among sober drivers than among drivers who had been drinking, and it wasn’t concentrated at night. If this were really about release parties and alcohol, you’d expect the opposite on all three counts.”
Patel told The Harvard Gazette that his own behavior after his wife texted him to listen to a song inspired the study.
He started looking through his phone, and a few moments later he realized he was swerving out of his lane. That’s when he concluded there must be a huge cumulative danger on the road if millions of others are doing the same thing on the day a major album drops.
“We don’t know for sure what the mechanism is here. Is it that the music is louder? Is it that it’s a new album, and people are just excited to hear it? Is it the mechanics of it all, meaning you’re fumbling around with your phone trying to download something?” said Dr. Anupam Jena, a professor at Harvard Medical School and a co-author of the study.
In conclusion, the researchers said the “study highlights how the potential impact of smartphone use on distracted driving can be assessed by studying changes in traffic fatalities during periods when smartphone use dramatically increases, leveraging plausibly exogenous variation in when rather than by whom smartphones are used.”

sources.news_title: Major Pop Album Releases Coincide With Spikes in Car Accident Deaths
sources.text:
That New Taylor Swift Hit Could Raise Your Risk of a Serious Car Crash
The rush you feel when listening to a just-released album from your favorite artist can be transporting. But it can also be distracting: New research suggests this distraction might increase the risk of fatal car accidents.
“It came out of a near-miss,” says the lead study author, Vishal Patel, MD, MPH, a resident physician at Mass General Brigham and a clinical fellow at Harvard Medical School in Boston. One day, Dr. Patel’s wife texted him suggestions about new Taylor Swift songs to listen to after an album release. “I was driving, started scrolling through Spotify to find them, and looked up to find myself drifting out of my lane,” he says.
Patel already worked with the federal registry of fatal crashes. “I realized nobody had looked at album release days, which are one of the few moments when millions of people reach for their phones at once for something other than texting.” What he discovered, he says, was eye-opening.
Study Looked at Traffic Fatality Data Around 10 Major Album Release Dates
For the study, published in JAMA Network Open, researchers analyzed data from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), a population-based registry of fatal motor vehicle crashes in the United States. The researchers specifically looked at traffic fatalities in the 10 days before and after the release dates of the top 10 most-streamed albums from 2017 through 2022.
The data showed that daily music streaming spiked after major album releases, going from an average of 86.1 million daily plays to 123.3 million plays — a 43 percent increase.
During the six-year study period, there were more than 230,000 traffic fatalities in the United States. Victims were 44.3 years old on average, and the majority (nearly 72 percent) were male.
While the increased risk of fatalities varied by album release, the researchers found a 15.1 percent increase in traffic fatalities on album release days. Excess fatalities were higher among drivers who were younger, male, and driving alone. The weather was typically clear, no alcohol was involved, and the cars were more likely to have infotainment systems.
Taken together, the data suggest that online music streaming through smartphones may significantly contribute to distracted driving and traffic fatalities, the researchers wrote.
Among the Top 10 Major Albums, 3 Were From Taylor Swift
Scientists marked the difference between traffic fatalities on an album’s release day and the six same-weekday control days at one, two, and three weeks before and after the album’s release (provided they didn’t fall on a public holiday or within three days of another album’s release).
The album that coincided with the largest increase in fatalities was Her Loss by Drake and 21 Savage, followed by Kendrick Lamar’s Mr. Morale and Bad Bunny’s Un Verano Sin Ti.
Other albums linked with an increase in traffic fatalities, from the largest increase to the smallest, were:
- Scorpion by Drake
- Harry’s House by Harry Styles
- Certified Lover Boy by Drake
- Folklore by Taylor Swift
- Red (Taylor’s Version) by Taylor Swift
- Midnights by Taylor Swift
The release of Kanye West’s Donda was the only album linked to a decrease in traffic fatalities.
2 Distractions Happen at Once With Streaming Music
Distracted driving is probably the biggest reason for this association, Patel says. But he notes that there are two kinds of distraction happening with streaming music. “There’s the manual part — unlocking the phone, opening the app, scrolling a new tracklist, tapping the right song — which takes eyes off the road and a hand off the wheel,” he says. “That’s several seconds of looking at a screen instead of the road.”
There’s also a different cognitive demand with streaming music. “Unfamiliar music demands more attention than a playlist you’ve heard a hundred times,” Patel says. “Notably, the increase in fatalities was actually larger in cars equipped with CarPlay, which suggests that making streaming easier to reach may increase how often drivers interact with it, even if each interaction is safer.”
That distraction can quickly turn deadly, says Robert Glatter, MD, an attending emergency medicine doctor at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City who was not involved in the new research. “At 60 miles per hour, a two-second glance covers roughly 175 feet of road completely unseen. Five seconds is well over a football field,” he says. “Glances away from the roadway longer than about two seconds sharply increase crash risk.”
Dr. Glatter says people underestimate what they are capable of doing while driving. “The brain doesn’t truly multitask; it switches, and switching costs time,” he says.
Distracted Driving Is Deadly
While many people dismiss the risks of distracted driving, experts stress that the dangers are real and significant.
Crashes linked to distracted driving tend to be especially dangerous because they often happen at full speed, Glatter says. “The full kinetic energy of the collision is transferred to the occupants, which translates into traumatic brain injury, cervical spine fractures, blunt aortic injury, and pelvic and solid organ trauma,” he says. “Survivors often face months of rehabilitation or permanent disability.”
How to Stream and Drive Safely, According to Doctors
Streaming music is a different kind of distraction than changing a radio station, which only requires you to push a button, Patel says. To lower your risks, experts recommend the following tactics.
- Set your playlist before you start driving. “Pick the album, hit play, and put the phone down,” Patel says.
- Let your passenger be the DJ. “That's the closest thing we found to a protective factor,” he says.
- Use voice commands if your car supports them. This can help you keep your eyes on the road.
- Save new music for time outside the car. “Novelty is exactly what makes a release-day album distracting,” Glatter says. “You’re skipping around, checking track names, reacting emotionally. Give it a first listen at home or as a passenger.”
New releases may be especially dangerous, according to Kite-Laidlaw. “While there’s nothing wrong with listening to music, especially if it helps you stay alert on a long and monotonous drive, a new release that commands all your attention should wait until you’re home,” she says. “If temptation is difficult to avoid, put the phone where you physically cannot reach it until you reach your destination.”
- Patel V et al. Smartphones, Online Music Streaming, and Traffic Fatalities. JAMA Network Open. August 17, 2026.
- Distracted Driving. National Safety Council.

When a blockbuster album drops, streaming numbers may not be the only thing that spikes.
A new study, published today in JAMA Network Open, finds traffic deaths also rise significantly.
Dr. Vishal Patel of Harvard Medical School and colleagues compared U.S. traffic fatalities on the release dates of 10 of the most-streamed albums from 2017 to 2022 with those in the 10 days before and after.
On release days, music streaming was 43% higher, and traffic fatalities were 15% higher.
In all, there were 139 deaths on release days, compared with 121 on surrounding days.
The study doesn't prove streaming caused the increase—or that the drivers involved were streaming music.
But the authors say, "These findings suggest that online music streaming through smartphones is associated with distracted driving and traffic fatalities."
Potential distractions include the phone, infotainment system—or even the music itself.
The researchers say the study raises a broader safety issue: As streaming becomes easier behind the wheel, could the convenience come with a hidden risk?

sources.news_title: Fans more likely to die on favourite band's album release day
sources.text:
Fans more likely to be killed in car accident when their favourite bands release a new album, according to science
Fontaines DC fans should buckle in, as even though the band might be on the verge of releasing their latest album, a new study has found that you may be more likely to die because of it.
Fresh research from Harvard University has found that music fans are at a higher risk of being involved in fatal car crashes on the day that their favourite artist releases a new album.
While the phenomenon obviously isn’t exclusive to the Irish rock band, amid a year that has already seen major releases from the likes of Harry Styles, Madonna, Phoebe Bridgers, and more, fans could be at a higher risk than ever.
According to The Guardian, research carried out by Dr Vishal Patel and his colleagues at the Harvard Medical School found that in a period of ten major album release days from 2017 to 2022, the number of fatal road traffic incidents that took place in the US increased by 15.1 per cent.
The albums featured in the study included the likes of Midnights by Taylor Swift and Harry’s House by Styles, both released in 2022, as well as Scorpion by Drake, released in 2018.
“Album releases give you something closer to an experiment – a day when smartphone use jumps nationally for reasons that have nothing to do with road conditions, weather or who happens to be driving,” Patel wrote in the Jama Network Open journal.
The study revealed that the streaming volume of the top 200 songs on Spotify in the US increased by 43 per cent on major album release days, and although there is no way of knowing whether music was playing at the time when car crashes occurred, this correlates to the heightened rate of fatalities.
“What it establishes is that these days are genuinely different in terms of national engagement with music, which is the premise the whole study rests on,” Patel added.
The researchers theorised that this is the case not only because new music is unfamiliar and commands more attention from the listener, but because the act of searching for a new album on a streaming service takes more time than usual, thus distracting the driver from the road for longer.
“Online music streaming through smartphones may significantly contribute to distracted driving and traffic fatalities,” the study concluded.
Ultimately, Patel had some important advice to music fans getting behind the wheel on a big album release day. “Pick the album, hit play, put the phone down,” he said. “If someone’s in the passenger seat, hand it to them – the increase showed up almost entirely among drivers who were alone.”

sources.news_title: When big albums start streaming, traffic deaths surge
sources.text:
When Dr. Vishal Patel found himself scrolling through Spotify to find songs from a new Taylor Swift album in his car, he realized he had drifted out of his lane.
It’s a situation many drivers find themselves in, searching for the perfect song to add to their queues, and the moment inspired Patel, a physician at Mass General Brigham and researcher at Harvard Medical School, to look into whether car crash fatalities increase when major artists release new albums.
More than 35,000 people die in car crashes in the US each year, according to the US Department of Transportation, with millions injured. In 2022, there were 3,308 fatalities in crashes due to distracted driving.
Patel’s new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Network Open, found a 15% increase in traffic fatalities on the days major new albums are released, compared with the days immediately before and after.
New music, more phone usage
Distracted driving is “genuinely hard” to study, Patel said, as most of the research in the space comes from self-reporting drivers or driving simulators.
The researchers found that when popular artists released albums, there would also be an increase in general phone usage, and one reason may be because people are looking to stream the album on their phones. They identified the top 10 most streamed albums in a single day from 2017 to 2022, including “Midnights” by Taylor Swift, “Certified Lover Boy” by Drake and “Un Verano Sin Ti” by Bad Bunny and others by Harry Styles, Kendrick Lamar and Kanye West.
The study looked at a 10-day window before and after an album release to address concerns that there may have been more car crashes on specific days of the week. The researchers also examined fatal crashes, looking at drivers’ ages, alcohol involvement, the number of people in the car and the model year of cars, as newer cars may have more safety features that prevent distraction.
The study used the Fatality Analysis Reporting System, a nationwide census from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, to collect population-based data on fatal car crashes on public roads in the US, along with daily music streaming data from Spotify, a music streaming platform that is used by about 29% of US residents ages 12 and older.
“I already knew the FARS database well; it’s the federal registry of every fatal crash on US roads, and there’s a long tradition of using it to ask whether crashes spike on Super Bowl Sunday or Tax Day,” Patel said. “It struck me that nobody had looked at album releases, which are one of the few moments when tens of millions of people reach for their phones at the same time, for the same reason, for something other than texting.”
Increased fatalities on album release dates
There were about 18 more deaths on the release days of the albums in the study. On average, the study found that there were 121 car crash fatalities on non-album release dates, compared with 139 deaths on album release days. The number of deaths was larger for younger drivers than older drivers.
“What convinced me it was real was the pattern underneath it,” Patel said. “The increase showed up mostly among drivers who were alone in the car, it was more pronounced among sober drivers than among drivers who had been drinking, and it wasn’t concentrated at night. If this were really about release parties and alcohol, you’d expect the opposite on all three counts.”
The researchers acknowledged that there may also be external factors causing traffic fatalities on the same day an album releases and that Spotify is not the only music platform drivers may use.
Patel said FARS data can show car crash fatalities but cannot confirm that drivers were on their phones at the time of the crash.
“We don’t know for sure what the mechanism is here. Is it that the music is louder? Is it that it’s a new album, and people are just excited to hear it? Is it the mechanics of it all, meaning you’re fumbling around with your phone trying to download something?” said Dr. Anupam Jena, a professor at Harvard Medical School and a co-author of the study.
The study also does not consider impacts of album releases on nonfatal crashes, but it does take into account federal holidays, which also have increased car crash fatalities.
Ian Reagan, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety who was not involved with the study, said although researchers control for federal holidays, they do not take into account other holidays, like Halloween, that may increase car crash fatalities.
“If people, if states were celebrating Halloween that weekend as opposed to the weekend beforehand, that could account for things,” Reagan said.
Patel said the goal of the study isn’t to tell people to stop listening to music in the car
“It’s that these days are predictable,” Patel said.
Staying focused despite more distractions
For years, conversations about distracted driving have focused on texting and phone calls, said Dr. Despina Stavrinos, director at the Institute of Social Science Research at the University of Alabama. But newer technology has added more pathways for drivers to interact with their phones, including navigation, voice assistants and social media.
“This study broadens the conversation from, ‘Are people texting while driving?’ to a much more important question: How does continuous interaction with a digital ecosystem affect driving?” Stavrinos said in an email.
Something that “seems simple,” like choosing a song, requires drivers to make a decision, interact with their phones and then refocus on the road, said Stavrinos, who was not involved with the new research.
“It is whether the technology is competing with the attentional resources needed to safely operate the vehicle,” she said.
People can minimize distractions in their car by turning off their phones, putting them in a bag so they’re not accessible, turning on “do not disturb” mode or asking a passenger to interact with the phone if needed, said Stephanie Payne, a professor of psychology at Texas A&M University who was not involved with the new research.
“We rely on our phones for communication and information so much that it is difficult to go for extended periods of time without interacting with them. To complicate things further, notifications are really hard to ignore,” Payne said.
Dr. Christopher Worsham, an assistant professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and a co-author of the new study, said other studies look at the potential for music to be distracting, but it is unrealistic for many to drive in silence.
“Our study suggests that the dangerous part here is the fiddling with the phone or the infotainment system, not the listening. Changing the music on touch screens in the car, which is very common now, is different than pushing a button without taking your eyes off the road,” Worsham said. “Queue up your music before you put the car in drive, and let it play until you can safely change it.”

sources.news_title: Traffic Deaths Rise 15% on Days Major Albums Are Released, Study Finds
Smartphones, Online Music Streaming, and Traffic Fatalities Linked in New
sources.text:
A new cross-sectional study of traffic fatalities in the United States has identified a striking association between major music album releases and a short-term rise in fatal crashes. The research, published in JAMA Network Open, suggests that periods when highly anticipated albums become available—and when online music streaming increases—may coincide with more deaths on the road. The findings raise fresh concerns about how smartphone-based listening habits could influence driver attention, particularly when people search for new releases, select songs, adjust playlists, or interact with streaming applications while driving.
The study focuses on a modern form of distracted driving that is less visible than texting but may involve many of the same cognitive and manual demands. Streaming music through a smartphone can require drivers to unlock a device, navigate an app, browse recommendations, search for an artist, choose an album, skip tracks, or change playback settings. Even when a driver is not typing a message, these actions can divert visual attention from the road, occupy one or both hands, and disrupt the mental processing needed to monitor traffic conditions. Researchers examined whether major album releases, which can produce sudden increases in listening activity, were associated with measurable changes in traffic fatalities across the United States.
The analysis used a cross-sectional design, meaning that it compared patterns in traffic deaths with patterns in album-release timing and music-streaming activity rather than following individual drivers over time. This type of study can identify population-level associations, especially when an exposure affects large numbers of people at roughly the same time. A major release provides a naturally occurring event that may cause a sharp increase in the number of people opening a streaming service or interacting with music apps. By examining traffic outcomes around these events, investigators sought to determine whether fatal crashes increased during periods of intensified online music consumption.
The results indicate that major album releases were associated with a significant increase in traffic fatalities. The association was accompanied by increased online streaming, supporting the possibility that smartphone-based music activity may be one pathway connecting new releases with crash risk. The study does not establish that streaming caused every additional death, nor does it demonstrate that all listeners were using their phones while driving. Instead, it points to a population-level signal: when music consumption rises rapidly after a prominent release, fatal traffic outcomes appear to rise as well. That signal is important because even a modest increase in risk can translate into a substantial number of deaths when millions of drivers are exposed.
Driving requires the continuous integration of visual, motor, and cognitive information. A driver must detect changes in speed, position, and direction; predict the behavior of other road users; and respond quickly to unexpected hazards. Smartphone interaction can interfere with these processes through several mechanisms. Visual distraction occurs when a driver looks away from the roadway, manual distraction occurs when the driver handles a device, and cognitive distraction occurs when attention is absorbed by a task unrelated to driving. Music streaming can involve all three. A person who spends only a few seconds searching for an album may miss a braking vehicle, a pedestrian, a cyclist, or a changing traffic signal. At highway speeds, a brief glance away can cover a considerable distance before the driver looks back.
The findings also illustrate why distracted driving may be underestimated when public attention focuses primarily on texting. Music applications are often perceived as benign because listening itself does not require active interaction. However, the process of choosing what to hear can be highly interactive, especially when a new album has just been released and users are motivated to find it immediately. Streaming platforms are designed for rapid browsing and personalization, with interfaces that encourage users to scroll through recommendations, open artist pages, compare tracks, and respond to notifications. The convenience of these systems may unintentionally make it easier for drivers to engage with their phones during trips.
Because the study examined aggregate data, several explanations must be considered. Major releases may occur on particular days of the week, during holidays, or in seasons when travel patterns differ. New albums may also be promoted alongside concerts, festivals, nightlife, or other events that could alter the number of people on the road. Weather, road construction, fuel prices, sporting events, alcohol consumption, traffic volume, and changes in enforcement could all influence crash fatalities. A cross-sectional association cannot fully distinguish the effect of music streaming from these other factors. The researchers’ finding that the increase in streaming accompanied the increase in fatalities strengthens the plausibility of the proposed mechanism, but it does not remove the possibility of residual confounding.
The study nevertheless carries practical implications for drivers, technology companies, policymakers, and public-health officials. Drivers can reduce risk by selecting music before starting a journey, using voice controls when appropriate, enabling driving modes that limit notifications, and placing smartphones out of reach. Streaming services could design interfaces that restrict browsing while a device is moving, automatically activate safer playback settings, or make it easier to begin listening without prolonged interaction. Vehicle manufacturers and regulators could also consider how smartphone integration systems manage music selection and whether their interfaces promote safe use. Public-health campaigns may benefit from expanding the definition of distracted driving to include music discovery and playlist management, not only messaging and phone calls.
The research comes from Anupam B. Jena, MD, PhD, of the Department of Health Care Policy at Harvard Medical School, and colleagues. Its broader message is that emerging digital behaviors can create safety risks before society fully recognizes them. Music streaming is now deeply integrated into daily transportation, and the same devices used for navigation, communication, and entertainment are often used behind the wheel. As streaming platforms continue to personalize recommendations and release music simultaneously to global audiences, sudden bursts of user engagement may become increasingly common. The study does not suggest that listening to music while driving is inherently dangerous. Rather, it indicates that interacting with a smartphone to access music may carry consequences that extend beyond the individual user—and that preventing those interactions could be an overlooked opportunity to reduce traffic deaths.
Subject of Research: Association between major music album releases, online music streaming, smartphone use, distracted driving, and traffic fatalities in the United States.
